dialog.body: Public Works, this is Lorraine. Good afternoon.

Yeah, hi, good afternoon. This is Leo Lombardozzi. I own a couple of units up on Ayrault Street, and I got a situation here with, well, with water in the street. Which is strange, because it hasn't rained in what, a week? Maybe more. My tenant said Sunday was dry as a bone.
Okay, Mr. Lombardozzi. Water in the street, and no rain lately. Can you tell me where exactly you're seeing it?

Three seventy-one Ayrault Street. Right at the corner there, up the Hill. Historic Hill, you know. My father bought that building in, oh, it must've been the seventies, and back then the whole street had these big old iron grates, you could lose a shoe in them. Anyway. Where was I. The corner.
Three seventy-one Ayrault Street, at the corner. And what is it you're seeing at the corner?

So the drain grate, the one in the street by the corner, it's froze shut. Solid ice on top of it, all around the edges. And the water's coming from somewhere, I don't even know, maybe a leak up the street, and it can't go down, so it just spreads. It's across the whole intersection now, a big sheet of it.
So the grate is frozen over, and the water is pooling and spreading across the intersection. Is it moving toward anybody's property, or is it just in the roadway?

Just the road so far, and the sidewalk on my side, edge of it. But it's freezing again at night, that's what worries me. It's four o'clock, it's gonna be dark by quarter to five, and then it's black ice all over that corner. And there's kids that come through there, going home from the school bus, and people walking dogs all the time. A lady with a little white dog, she's out there every day. A kid slips out there, into the road, I don't even want to think about it.
I understand. So the concern is kids and dog walkers near the water, and it icing over once the sun goes down. Let me get that noted.

Yeah. Exactly. And I'm not blaming anybody, I just, who do I call to get it checked? I didn't know if it's you, or the water department, or what. Last time I called about something it was a different office altogether. That was about a tree limb, years ago, and they sent me around three places.

You called the right place. Storm drains and street drainage come through Public Works, so I'll put in a request for a crew to look at it. If it turns out to be a water line leaking, they'll pass it along to the right people.

Okay, good. Good. Because I thought maybe it was a main or something. Hey, can I ask you something totally unrelated? My printer, it's been offline two days now. For no reason. I didn't touch anything. It says offline, the computer sees nothing. I was gonna print the lease for the upstairs tenant. Is that, you wouldn't know anything about that, would you?
Ha, no, I'm afraid that's not something we handle here. Sorry, Mr. Lombardozzi. Maybe try unplugging it for a minute and plugging it back in.
Yeah, I did that. Twice. Okay, never mind, my fault for asking. Back to the street. So what happens now?

Let me read back what I have. Three seventy-one Ayrault Street, Historic Hill, at the corner intersection. Storm drain grate frozen shut, water spreading across the intersection with no recent rain, and it's a concern for ice after dark and for pedestrians. Is that right?
That's it. That's all of it.
Good. Do you want a call back once someone's been out? I can put a number on it.
Sure, sure. It's four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-nine-two. That's the landline, I'm here most days.

Four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-nine-two. Got it. I'm sending this over to the crew supervisor now, and I'm marking it as a safety concern because of the ice. If it gets worse before anybody gets there, call us right back.
I will. Thank you, Lorraine. I appreciate it. I just don't want somebody getting hurt on my corner.
Understood. Take care, Mr. Lombardozzi.
You too. Bye now.
